evidence_item.title: Later biblical identification of the ancient serpent
evidence_item.description: Revelation 12:9 later identifies the “ancient serpent” with the devil and Satan. This is later canonical reception and does not make Genesis 3 itself use those names.
evidence_item.confidence_rationale: The two texts state different things directly; their canonical relation is later reception.
evidence_item.passage_relevance: Revelation 12:9 later identifies the “ancient serpent” with the devil and Satan. This is later canonical reception and does not make Genesis 3 itself use those names. This supports passage-specific synthesis of Genesis 3 while preserving the stated limits.
evidence_item.primary_observation: Genesis 3:1 describes the serpent without naming Satan; Revelation 12:9 explicitly uses the later identification.
evidence_item.scholarly_interpretation: The later text can inform canonical readings while remaining distinct from the serpent’s characterization in the immediate Genesis narrative.

related_objects.notes: The later reception refers to the serpent in Genesis 3.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The Genesis wording names the serpent but not Satan.

evidence_item.title: Later Jewish and Christian reception of Genesis 3:15
evidence_item.description: Pentateuchal Targums and New Testament reception read Genesis 3:15’s enmity as a conflict between serpent and adversarial powers; Revelation 12 develops a later serpent-conflict image. These are later interpretations and do not replace the immediate offspring language.
evidence_item.confidence_rationale: The later reception is documented in a focused comparative study and is distinguished from Genesis wording.
evidence_item.passage_relevance: Pentateuchal Targums and New Testament reception read Genesis 3:15’s enmity as a conflict between serpent and adversarial powers; Revelation 12 develops a later serpent-conflict image. These are later interpretations and do not replace the immediate offspring language. This supports passage-specific synthesis of Genesis 3 while preserving the stated limits.
evidence_item.primary_observation: Genesis 3:15 gives the immediate enmity wording; later Targumic and Christian texts interpret that conflict in expanded ways.
evidence_item.scholarly_interpretation: Zhakevich’s comparative study documents these readings as reception history. Messianic interpretation is therefore recorded as a later Jewish/Christian reading, not the only original meaning supplied to synthesis.

related_objects.notes: The reception interprets the serpent and enmity in Genesis 3.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The immediate wording remains the anchor.

evidence_item.title: Cherubim as guardians and biblical sacred-space figures
evidence_item.description: Genesis 3:24 stations cherubim east of the garden to guard the way to the tree of life. Later biblical sanctuary texts place cherubim over or within sacred settings; Genesis 3 does not describe their physical appearance.
evidence_item.confidence_rationale: Genesis’s guarding role is explicit; the wider biblical sacred-space pattern is comparative context.
evidence_item.passage_relevance: Genesis 3:24 stations cherubim east of the garden to guard the way to the tree of life. Later biblical sanctuary texts place cherubim over or within sacred settings; Genesis 3 does not describe their physical appearance. This supports passage-specific synthesis of Genesis 3 while preserving the stated limits.
evidence_item.primary_observation: Genesis gives the cherubim a guarding function; Exodus 25:18–22 and 1 Kings 6:23–35 provide later sanctuary context.
evidence_item.scholarly_interpretation: Lexham’s entry discusses guardian and sanctuary/throne associations. This context excludes later popular “baby angel” imagery but does not establish a single appearance for Genesis 3.

related_objects.notes: The cherubim guard the route back into Eden.

evidence_item.notes: Comparative biblical sanctuary context (not Genesis applicability anchors): Exodus 25:18–22 places cherubim over the ark; 1 Kings 6:23–35 describes cherubim in the temple. These later texts contextualize Genesis 3:24 but do not establish a single physical appearance for Eden’s cherubim. Comparative Scripture sources retained: g1-exodus-text and g1-kings-text; scholarly context source retained: g1-lexham-cherubim.
